```{r requires, echo = FALSE, message = FALSE}
library (igraph)
```


## Network Software {#standards-networks}

Network software implements algorithms which analyse, construct, or transform
data representing relationships between discrete entities. These entities are
referred to here as "vertices" (or "nodes"), and their relationships as "edges"
(or "links"). Network software is frequently developed for domain-specific
use-cases, such as for transport systems, social networks, or genomic data, but
is considered here to include any software for which the primary inputs and/or
outputs represent networks in some form.

The following standards proceed according to the assumption that network
software performs some or all of the following steps:

1. Accept and validate input data
2. Apply one or more analytic algorithms
3. Return the result of that algorithmic application
4. Offer additional functionality such as printing, summarising, or plotting
   return results
5. Testing

Each standard for network software is prefixed with "**NW**".

### Documentation

Even when network software is intended to enable truly general use, the
following standard applies.

- [**NW1.0**]{#NW1_0} *Network software should explicitly indicate its domain
  of applicability, generally as a broad description of applicable academic (or
  equivalent) domains.*

Authors are encouraged to include as many *potentially* applicable or relevant
domains as possible, even if application in such domains has been neither tried
nor demonstrated. Authorial statements of potential applicability are one of
the clearest ways to encourage usage of software beyond the initial domains for
which it might have been developed.

- [**NW1.1**]{#NW1_1} *Network software should document scaling relationships
  between sizes of input data (numbers of vertices, edges, or both) and
  algorithmic speed, and describe the expected range of data size for which the
  software is usable.*

This documentation may be placed anywhere, including in a dedicated vignette,
but should at least be referenced from a primary location such as the main
README file.

Networks differ in properties which fundamentally alter the meaning and
validity of many algorithms. The following two standards concern documentation
of those properties.

- [**NW1.2**]{#NW1_2} *Network software should document the types of networks
  to which its algorithms may be applied, including whether networks may be
  directed or undirected, weighted or unweighted, and may contain self-loops or
  multiple edges between the same pair of vertices. Software should further
  document whether networks are assumed to be connected, and how disconnected
  components and isolated vertices are treated.*
- [**NW1.3**]{#NW1_3} *Network software which accepts edge weights should
  document how those weights are interpreted; for example, whether larger
  weights denote stronger connections, or greater distances or costs; or
  whether weights must be strictly positive.*

Interpretation of weights is a common source of error. A shortest-path
algorithm, for example, treats weights as costs, while many clustering
algorithms treat them as strengths of association, and passing the same weights
to each yields entirely different results.


### Input Data Structures and Validation

Most network software is intended to accept networks as input parameters. This
is nevertheless not always the case, and many of the following standards may
not apply to software which transforms non-network inputs into internal network
representations. The following two sub-sections will generally be mutually
exclusive, and software will either accept class-based inputs, and so comply
with the standards in the following sub-section, or it will accept generic
inputs, and so comply with the standards in the sub-section after that. The
standards in the remaining sub-sections apply to both.

#### Class-based inputs

R has a number of widely used packages for representing and analysing networks.
The following standard reflects one aim of rOpenSci to curate an interoperable
"ecosystem" of software:

- [**NW2.0**]{#NW2_0} *Where possible or practicable, network software should
  either represent network data using a common representation, or at least
  prominently demonstrate how to convert package-internal representations to
  common forms.*

"Common representations" refer to the types offered by widely-used packages for
network representation and/or analyses, including but not limited to the
packages [`igraph`](https://igraph.org),
[`tidygraph`](https://tidygraph.data-imaginist.com/),
[`network`](https://github.com/statnet/network), or
[`sfnetworks`](https://luukvdmeer.github.io/sfnetworks/) for spatial networks.

- [**NW2.1**]{#NW2_1} *Network software which accepts networks as inputs should
  explicitly indicate the expected forms of those networks.*
- [**NW2.2**]{#NW2_2} *Submitting inputs in any common class beyond those
  accepted by network software should result in error messages providing
  helpful information on how to convert to appropriate classes.*


#### Generic input structures

Network software may accept generic inputs which do not rely on specific class
structures. Network representations may be edge-based, "standard" graph-based
representations, or matrix-based. The following standards apply to generic
input structures.

- [**NW2.3**]{#NW2_3} *Network software which accepts generic input structures
  (such as matrices) should implement initial validation routines to ensure the
  internal properties of input data conform with expectations.*

Expectations implied by this standard include those related to types or ranges
of input data, such as strictly binary values for adjacency matrices.
Expectations regarding missing values are addressed separately in **NW2.6**.

- [**NW2.4**]{#NW2_4} *Network software which accepts generic input structures
  should document, and where input permits should assert, expectations on
  whether networks are directed, and whether they may contain self-loops or
  multiple edges. In particular, adjacency matrices intended to represent
  undirected networks should be confirmed to be symmetric.*
- [**NW2.5**]{#NW2_5} *Network software which accepts edge-based input should
  validate that all vertices referenced by edges are consistent with any
  separately specified vertex data, and that each edge is fully specified by
  both of its end points.*

Missing and undefined values are covered by the General Standards **G2.13**--
**G2.16**. The following standard describes the additional network-specific
considerations:

- [**NW2.6**]{#NW2_6} *In addition to the requirements of **G2.13**--**G2.16**,
  network software which accepts generic input structures should implement
  explicit parameters controlling the processing of missing values, and should
  document how a missing value is distinguished from an absent edge. Where
  possible, `NA` or `NaN` values should be distinguished from `Inf` values in
  edge weights. Network structures able to be specified in matrix form should
  permit and appropriately process missing values (even where appropriate
  processing is to error on missing values).*
- [**NW2.7**]{#NW2_7} *For matrix-based representations, documentation should
  explicitly describe and/or demonstrate whether sparse representations are
  used or permitted.*

#### Pre-processing of inputs

Standard **G2.8** requires that all sub-functions of a package receive inputs
of a single defined class or type. The following standards extend that
requirement to the specific properties of networks.

- [**NW2.8**]{#NW2_8} *Network software should implement a single
  pre-processing routine to validate input data, and to appropriately transform
  it to a single uniform type to be passed to all subsequent data-processing
  functions.*

This function may even be applicable to software accepting class-based inputs,
in which a pre-processing routine should still be called to validate the
expected form and properties of any input.

- [**NW2.9**]{#NW2_9} *This pre-processing function should maintain metadata
  attributes of input data which are relevant or important to core algorithms
  or return values.*

These metadata attributes include labels discussed in the following
sub-section, but may also include additional data such as numbers of vertices
and edges, timestamps, data sources, or any metadata necessary or useful for
appropriate interpretation of results.


#### Labels on input data

Network software often implements algorithms which identify or operate on
discrete sub-sets of a network, such as identifying discrete groups or clusters
of edges or vertices. In such cases, the membership of vertices or edges within
discrete groups is important, and is generally denoted by some kind of label.
The following standards apply to software which transfers attributes of input
data used to label vertices or edges on to output data.

- [**NW2.10**]{#NW2_10} *Network software should transfer all relevant aspects
  of input data, notably including row and column names, and potentially
  information from other attributes (such as vertex or edge labels), to
  corresponding aspects of return objects.*
    - [**NW2.10a**]{#NW2_10a} *Where otherwise relevant information is not
      transferred, this should be explicitly documented, or informative
      diagnostic messages should be issued.*

The following code provides an example of default behaviour in response to
input which has no properties or attributes to be transferred, beginning by
constructing a random binary adjacency matrix with pairwise connections set to
`TRUE` for adjacent vertices.

```{r bin-nb-mat, echo = TRUE}
n_verts <- 10L
edge_density <- 1 # Mean number edges per vertex
set.seed (1L)
nbs <- array (FALSE, dim = c (n_verts, n_verts))
nbs [sample (n_verts ^ 2, size = n_verts * edge_density)] <- TRUE
```

The following code then constructs an `igraph` graph from that adjacency
matrix, and enumerates the connected components of that graph.

```{r igraph-adj-no-labels, echo = TRUE}
library (igraph)
g <- graph_from_adjacency_matrix (nbs)
components (g)
```

The result of [the `igraph` components
function](https://igraph.org/r/html/latest/components.html) includes a
"membership" vector with `n_verts` values, such that `membership[1]` gives the
group membership of the first vertex. Vertices in the above code were
unlabelled, and the "membership" values simply enumerate the groups from "1"
for the largest to, in this case, "3" for the smallest. This enumeration also
illustrates the documentation of group ordering required by **NW4.7**.

The following code demonstrates what happens when the input adjacency matrix is
labelled.

```{r igraph-adj-with-labels, echo = TRUE}
rownames (nbs) <- colnames (nbs) <- LETTERS [seq (nrow (nbs))]
g <- graph_from_adjacency_matrix (nbs)
components (g)
```

The row and column names of the input adjacency matrix are transferred to
labels of the resultant output data, demonstrating that this aspect of the
`igraph` package complies with standard **NW2.10**.

- [**NW2.11**]{#NW2_11} *Network software which uses attributes of input data
  such as row or column names to label output objects should assert that input
  data have non-default row or column names, and issue an informative message
  when these are not provided.*

The first example above represents code which would comply with this standard,
because passing an *unlabelled* input yields a correspondingly unlabelled
output. If, however, the output from an unlabelled input was a *labelled*
membership vector, then compliance with this standard would require issuing a
message that default labels had been used.

- [**NW2.12**]{#NW2_12} *Network software for which input data does not
  generally include labels (such as array-like data with no row or column
  names) should provide an ability to specify labels.*

This standard may also be illustrated with a modified version of the code
above, starting by removing the row and column labels from the adjacency
matrix, and then adding labels to the vertices of the resultant graph.

```{r igraph-labels-afterwards, echo = TRUE}
rownames (nbs) <- colnames (nbs) <- NULL
g <- graph_from_adjacency_matrix (nbs) # graph with no labels
V (g)$name <- LETTERS [seq (vcount (g))]
components (g)
```

Vertices of an `igraph` graph can be labelled by assigning to [the `name`
attribute of
`V(g)`](https://igraph.org/r/html/latest/vertex_attr-set.html), and those
labels are carried over to the output as in the previous example. This facility
would thus satisfy the **NW2.12** standard.



### Data Structures

- [**NW3.0**]{#NW3_0} *Network software which at any stage uses sparse matrix
  representations (or uses classes which are sparse in structure) should avoid
  converting to full matrix representations. In other words, sparse
  representations should be maintained throughout.*

Where this standard can not be fulfilled, clear explanations should be given
for the necessity of converting from sparse to full representations.

- [**NW3.1**]{#NW3_1} *Where possible, adjacency matrices should be
  represented in sparse formats (such as from the `Matrix` package or other
  sparse classes), and not as full matrices.*

Even where authors envision software to have a specific scope in which they
know matrices may be generally "small", the use of sparse representations is
the best way to ensure the software will readily extend to larger input sizes.

### Algorithms

- [**NW4.0**]{#NW4_0} *Software which represents networks as matrices, and
  which implements algorithms in C++, should generally use widely available
  libraries for matrix representation and manipulation.*

Examples of such libraries include [the
Armadillo](http://arma.sourceforge.net/) and
[Eigen](https://eigen.tuxfamily.org/) libraries, generally via R couplings such
as [the
`RcppArmadillo`](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/RcppArmadillo/index.html)
and [`RcppEigen`](https://dirk.eddelbuettel.com/code/rcpp.eigen.html) packages.

- [**NW4.1**]{#NW4_1} *Re-implementation of network-specific routines which
  exist in other commonly-used packages should explain, at least in code
  comments, the reasons for re-implementation.*
    - [**NW4.1a**]{#NW4_1a} *Where the reason for re-implementation is an
      improved implementation, this must be demonstrated, at least in tests.*

Reasons for re-implementation may be as simple as wanting to avoid extra
package dependencies, or more complex reasons such as desire to implement a
parallel version of an algorithm.

#### Iteration in algorithms

Many network packages contain ways of "fitting" models to data, and such
fitting procedures are often iterative. The following standards apply to any
iterative procedures implemented within network software.

- [**NW4.2**]{#NW4_2} *Loops intended to run until convergence should always
  implement a parameter controlling maximum number of iterations.*
- [**NW4.3**]{#NW4_3} *Where iterative fitting procedures are used, these
  should either:*
    - [**NW4.3a**]{#NW4_3a} *Include code comments which clearly explain why
      iteration always converges*; or
    - [**NW4.3b**]{#NW4_3b} *Include code to detect (potential)
      non-convergence, and terminate iteration. Where termination conditions
      are not user-controlled, code comments should also explain and justify
      parameter values.*
- [**NW4.4**]{#NW4_4} *Where iterative fitting procedures are used, code should
  explicitly count numbers of iterations, with resultant values able to be
  returned directly from function calls (although not necessarily by
  default).*
    - [**NW4.4a**]{#NW4_4a} *Routines which use an internally fixed number of
      maximal iterations should include a note justifying the value chosen.*
- [**NW4.5**]{#NW4_5} *Any exhaustive loops over multiple dimensions (> 1) of
  network matrices should generally be implemented in C/C++, or other efficient
  languages commonly placed in the `/src` sub-directory.*

The adjective "generally" in the previous standard leaves scope for this
standard not to be complied with, for example if a package has no other `/src`
code, and only implements one such loop. It should nevertheless be considered
bad practice to implement pairwise loops over all edges or vertices of a
network in R.

#### Stochastic algorithms

Many network algorithms, including those which generate random networks, sample
from networks, or search heuristically for optimal solutions, have random
components.

- [**NW4.6**]{#NW4_6} *Network software which includes any stochastic component
  should document the nature of that component, and should enable users to
  control it, for example through a seed parameter or by respecting the state
  of the random number generator in the calling environment.*


#### Network "grouping" Algorithms

The following standards apply to network software which discerns discrete
internal groups, such as clustering or dimensionality reduction algorithms.

- [**NW4.7**]{#NW4_7} *Network software should document how the ordering of
  groups is determined, and should explicitly state whether or not ordering is
  deterministic.*
    - [**NW4.7a**]{#NW4_7a} *Software in which ordering or labels are not
      deterministic should document how users can set seeds or other parameters
      in order to obtain stable groups and/or labels.*

The code demonstrated above can be again used to illustrate compliance with
this standard for a deterministic grouping algorithm. The groups are labelled
in the "membership" vector as discrete integers, with "1" denoting the largest
group; "2" the second largest; and so on. Adherence with this standard would
require documenting this labelling procedure.

- [**NW4.8**]{#NW4_8} *Network software which discerns groups should document
  whether groups are disjoint or may overlap, whether every vertex or edge must
  belong to a group, and how isolated vertices are assigned.*



### Return Objects and Generic Methods

- [**NW5.0**]{#NW5_0} *Return objects from network software should contain
  metadata on input networks, minimally including numbers of vertices and
  edges.*
- [**NW5.1**]{#NW5_1} *Network software may enable an ability to construct an
  empty return object (at no computational cost). This may be useful in
  controlling batch processing of computationally intensive network
  algorithms.*
- [**NW5.2**]{#NW5_2} *Network software should implement default `print`
  methods for return objects.*
- [**NW5.3**]{#NW5_3} *The default print method should always ensure only
  a restricted portion of the full results are printed to the screen.*
- [**NW5.4**]{#NW5_4} *Network software which returns some kind of models as
  outputs should also implement summary methods which should summarise the
  primary statistics used in generating the model (such as numbers of
  observations, parameters of methods applied). The summary method may also
  provide summary statistics from the resultant model.*

Network software which does not return model objects may of course also
implement `summary` methods complying with this standard.

- [**NW5.5**]{#NW5_5} *Network software may also provide default `plot` methods
  for return objects.*
- [**NW5.6**]{#NW5_6} *Objects returned from network software which labels,
  categorise, or partitions data into discrete groups should include, or
  provide immediate access to, quantitative information on intra-group
  variances or equivalent, as well as on inter-group relationships where
  applicable.*
- [**NW5.7**]{#NW5_7} *The return object from network software should include,
  or otherwise enable immediate extraction of, all parameters used to control
  the algorithm used.*
- [**NW5.8**]{#NW5_8} *Network software which returns networks as outputs
  should either return them in the same form as the corresponding inputs, or
  follow the guidance of **NW2.0** in using, or demonstrating conversion to,
  a common representation.*


#### Visualisation

- [**NW5.9**]{#NW5_9} *Network software which includes plotting routines should
  document and demonstrate visualisation methods, such as through a dedicated
  vignette. Where possible, such demonstrations should also include generation
  of interactive visualisations.*


### Testing

Network software should test the following properties and behaviours, in
addition to those required by the General Standards (**G5.0**--**G5.12**).

#### Input Structures

- [**NW6.0**]{#NW6_0} *Software which accepts multiple network classes should
  demonstrate that equivalent networks submitted in each class yield equivalent
  results, and that classes which are not accepted yield the expected error
  messages* (**NW2.0**--**NW2.2**).
- [**NW6.1**]{#NW6_1} *Software which accepts generic input structures should
  demonstrate that inputs violating each validation requirement are rejected
  with expected error messages; for example, non-binary or asymmetric
  adjacency matrices for undirected networks, or edges referencing vertices
  which do not exist* (**NW2.3**--**NW2.5**).
- [**NW6.2**]{#NW6_2} *Software which uses sparse representations should
  demonstrate that results from sparse input are identical to those from
  equivalent full representations, and that return objects retain sparse
  structure where documented* (**NW3.0**, **NW3.1**).

#### Output Labelling

With regard to labelling of output data, tests for network software should:

- [**NW6.3**]{#NW6_3} *Demonstrate that labels on input data are propagated to,
  or may be recovered from, output data* (**NW2.10**).
- [**NW6.4**]{#NW6_4} *Demonstrate that informative messages are issued where
  default labels are used for output data* (**NW2.11**).
- [**NW6.5**]{#NW6_5} *For grouping algorithms, demonstrate that the ordering
  of group labels follows the documented procedure, such as following
  decreasing group sizes* (**NW4.7**).
- [**NW6.6**]{#NW6_6} *For non-deterministic algorithms, demonstrate that
  results, including group labels, are stable when seeds are fixed* (**NW4.6**,
  **NW4.7a**).

#### Iteration

- [**NW6.7**]{#NW6_7} *Demonstrate that iterative routines terminate at the
  specified maximal number of iterations, and that cases of non-convergence are
  detected and reported* (**NW4.2**, **NW4.3**).
- [**NW6.8**]{#NW6_8} *Demonstrate that numbers of iterations are returned, and
  agree with expected values for trivial cases* (**NW4.4**).

#### Return Objects

The following standard tests the requirements for return objects described
above in the section on Return Objects and Generic Methods, and is general in
scope. It applies to all network software.

- [**NW6.9**]{#NW6_9} *Demonstrate that return objects contain the required
  metadata on input networks and all parameters used to control the algorithm*
  (**NW5.0**, **NW5.7**).

Compliance requires tests to examine the structure of return objects, not only
their numeric values (which are covered by the algorithmic tests below). Where
a return object is deliberately minimal, such as the empty objects permitted by
**NW5.1**, tests should demonstrate that the same metadata and parameters are
nevertheless present or recoverable.

#### Algorithmic Tests

The following extend the tests of statistical algorithms described in
**G5.4**--**G5.9**. These standards are general in scope, and apply to all
network software, although some are nevertheless conditional on the properties
of particular software. Tests of stochastic algorithms should additionally
follow **G5.5**, **G5.6b** and **NW6.6**.

- [**NW6.10**]{#NW6_10} **Network edge condition tests** *to demonstrate
  expected behaviour for extreme networks, including as a minimum: the empty
  network (no edges); networks with a single vertex; networks with isolated
  vertices or multiple disconnected components; networks with self-loops or
  multiple edges (where these are not prohibited); and complete networks*
  (extending **G5.8**).
- [**NW6.11**]{#NW6_11} **Benchmark network tests** *using networks with known
  properties, such as standard data sets from the literature or networks
  constructed to have analytically known results (for example, paths, cycles,
  stars, and complete networks), or generated by algorithms with known
  statistical properties* (extending **G5.0** and **G5.4**).
- [**NW6.12**]{#NW6_12} *Where results are expected to be mathematically
  consistent between directed and undirected representations of the same
  network, demonstrate that this is the case.*
- [**NW6.13**]{#NW6_13} *Network software should include tests which
  demonstrate and confirm the scaling of algorithmic efficiency with network
  size* (**NW1.1**).
- [**NW6.14**]{#NW6_14} *Demonstrate that results are invariant, or change
  only in the expected manner, when the order of vertices or edges in input data
  is permuted* (extending **G5.9**).
